label: prf:braiding-induced-ordering
title: Proof of braiding induced ordering
html:
Well-foundedness of \prec_c on W_n. Let S \subseteq W_n be non-empty.

(a) Degree is bounded below. Every w \in W_n has \ell(w) \geq 0. Let d = \min\{\ell(w) : w \in S\}. The set S_d = \{w \in S : \ell(w) = d\} is non-empty.

(b) Finite alphabet at each degree. Each w \in S_d is a word of length d over the finite alphabet \{1, \ldots, n-1\}. There are at most (n-1)^d such words, a finite set. Every finite totally ordered set has a minimum. Let w_0 be the lex-minimum of S_d.

(c) w_0 is the minimum of S. For any w \in S: if \ell(w) > d then w_0 \prec_c w (shorter words first); if \ell(w) = d then w_0 \leq_{\mathrm{lex}} w by construction. \square

Compatibility with concatenation. Let w \prec_c w' and u, v \in W_n. If \ell(w) < \ell(w') then \ell(u\,w\,v) < \ell(u\,w'\,v), since length is additive. If \ell(w) = \ell(w') and w <_{\mathrm{lex}} w', a common prefix u leaves the first differing letter unchanged, and so does a common suffix v, because w and w' have equal length and their first difference occurs before v begins. Hence u\,w\,v \prec_c u\,w'\,v. This is the admissibility condition of an (admissible system) on the free monoid; it uses only concatenation, not the quadratic or Yang--Baxter relations. \square

Neither part uses a braiding hypothesis.
